source_text: Ἔξεστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι· οὐ γὰρ παῖδες ἡμεῖς καὶ νήπιοι πρὸς τὸ παιδαριῶδες καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον τῆς μαθήσεως προσηγορεύμεθα, καθὼς οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι διαβεβλήκασιν· ἀναγεννηθέντες γοῦν εὐθέως τὸ τέλειον ἀπειλήφαμεν, οὗ ἕνεκεν ἐσπεύδομεν. ἐφωτίσθημεν γάρ· τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ἐπιγνῶναι τὸν θεόν. οὔκουν ἀτελὴς ὁ ἐγνωκὼς τὸ τέλειον. καί μου μὴ λάβησθε ὁμολογοῦντος ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεόν. ὧδέ πως γὰρ ἔδοξεν εἰπεῖν τῷ λόγῳ· ὃ δὲ ἐλεύθερος. αὐτίκα γοῦν βαπτιζομένῳ τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπ᾿ οὐρανῶν ἐπήχησε φωνὴ μάρτυς ἠγαπημένου »υἱός μου εἶ σὺ ἀγαπητός, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε.« πυθώμεθα οὖν τῶν σοφῶν· σήμερον ἀναγεννηθεὶς ὁ Χριστὸς ἤδη τέλειός ἐστιν ἤ, ὅπερ ἀτοπώτατον, ἐλλιπής. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, προσμαθεῖν τι αὐτῷ δεῖ. ἀλλὰ προσμαθεῖν μὲν αὐτὸν εἰκὸς οὐδὲ ἓν θεὸν ὄντα. οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲ μὴν διδάσκαλος τοῦ μόνου διδασκάλου. μή τι οὖν ὁμολογήσουσιν ἄκοντες τὸν λόγον, τέλειον ἐκ τελείου φύντα τοῦ πατρός, κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομικὴν προδιατύπωσιν ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείως; καὶ εἰ τέλειος ἦν, τί ἐβαπτίζετο ὁ τέλειος; ἔδει, φασί, πληρῶσαι τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. παγκάλως. φημὶ γάρ· ἅμα τοίνυν τῷ βαπτίζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου γίνεται τέλειος; δῆλον ὅτι. οὐδὲν οὖν πρὸς αὐτοῦ προσέμαθεν; οὐ γάρ. τελειοῦται δὲ τῷ λουτρῷ μόνῳ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τῇ καθόδῳ ἁγιάζεται; οὕτως ἔχει. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ συμβαίνει τοῦτο καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς, ὧν γέγονεν ὑπογραφὴ ὁ κύριος· βαπτιζόμενοι φωτιζόμεθα, φωτιζόμενοι υἱοποιούμεθα, υἱοποιούμενοι τελειούμεθα, τελειούμενοι ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα »ἐγώ«, φησίν, »εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες.« καλεῖται δὲ πολλαχῶς τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο, χάρισμα καὶ φώτισμα καὶ τέλειον καὶ λουτρόν· λουτρὸν μὲν δι᾿ οὗ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀπορρυπτόμεθα, χάρισμα δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν ἐπιτίμια ἀνεῖται, φώτισμα δὲ δι᾿ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον ἐκεῖνο φῶς τὸ σωτήριον ἐποπτεύεται, τουτέστιν δι᾿ οὗ τὸ θεῖον ὀξυωποῦμεν, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς φαμέν. τί γὰρ ἔτι λείπεται τῷ θεὸν ἐγνωκότι; καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον ὡς ἀληθῶς χάρισμα κεκλῆσθαι θεοῦ τὸ μὴ πεπληρωμένον· τέλειος δὲ ὢν τέλεια χαριεῖται δήπουθεν· ὡς δὲ ἅμα τῷ κελεῦσαι αὐτὸν πάντα γίνεται, οὕτως ἕπεται τῷ χαρίσασθαι μόνον βουληθῆναι αὐτὸν τὸ πεπληρῶσθαι τὴν χάριν. τὸ γὰρ μέλλον τοῦ χρόνου τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ θελήματος προλαμβάνεται. πρὸς δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ἀπαλλαγὴ σωτηρίας ἐστὶν ἀρχή. μόνον δὲ ἄρα οἱ πρῶτον δραξάμενοι τῶν ὅρων τῆς ζωῆς ἤδη τέλειοι, ζῶμεν δὲ ἤδη οἱ θανάτου κεχωρισμένοι. σωτηρία τοίνυν τὸ ἕπεσθαι Χριστῷ. »ὃ γὰρ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ, ζωή ἐστιν.« »ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν,« φησίν, »ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον καὶ εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν.« οὕτω τὸ πιστεῦσαι μόνον καὶ ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείωσίς ἐστιν ἐν ζωῇ· οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀσθενεῖ ὁ θεός. ὡς γὰρ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ἔργον ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦτο κόσμος ὀνομάζεται, οὕτως καὶ τὸ βούλημα αὐτοῦ ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶ σωτηρία καὶ τοῦτο ἐκκλησία κέκληται. οἶδεν οὖν οὓς κέκληκεν, οὓς δὲ κέκληκεν, σέσωκεν· κέκληκεν δὲ ἅμα καὶ σέσωκεν. »αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὑμεῖς«, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, »θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε.« οὐκ ἄρα θεμιτὸν ἡμῖν ἀτελὲς τὸ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ διδασκόμενον νοεῖν, τὸ δὲ μάθημα ἀίδιος σωτηρία ἀιδίου σωτῆρος, ᾧ ἡ χάρις εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ἀμήν. καὶ ὁ μόνον ἀναγεννηθείς, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τοὔνομα ἔχει, φωτισθεὶς ἀπήλλακται μὲν παραχρῆμα τοῦ σκότους, ἀπείληφεν δὲ αὐτόθεν τὸ φῶς. ὥσπερ οὖν οἱ τὸν ὕπνον ἀποσεισάμενοι εὐθέως ἔνδοθεν ἐγρηγόρασιν, μᾶλλον δὲ καθάπερ οἱ τὸ ὑπόχυμα τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν κατάγειν πειρώμενοι οὐ τὸ φῶς αὑτοῖς ἔξωθεν χορηγοῦσιν, ὃ οὐκ ἔχουσιν, τὸ δὲ ἐμπόδιον ταῖς ὄψεσι καταβιβάζοντες ἐλευθέραν ἀπολείπουσι τὴν κόρην, οὕτως καὶ οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι, τὰς ἐπισκοτούσας ἁμαρτίας τῷ θείῳ πνεύματι ἀχλύος δίκην ἀποτριψάμενοι, ἐλεύθερον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον καὶ φωτεινὸν ὄμμα τοῦ πνεύματος ἴσχομεν, ᾧ δὴ μόνῳ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύομεν, οὐρανόθεν ἐπεισρέοντος ἡμῖν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος· κρᾶμα τοῦτο αὐγῆς ἀιδίου τὸ ἀίδιον φῶς ἰδεῖν δυναμένης· ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅμοιον τῷ ὁμοίῳ φίλον, φίλον δὲ τὸ ἅγιον τῷ ἐξ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον, ὃ δὴ κυρίως κέκληται φῶς· »ἦτε γάρ ποτε σκότος, νῦν δὲ φῶς ἐν κυρίῳ.« ἐντεῦθεν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ τῶν παλαιῶν ἡγοῦμαι κεκλῆσθαι φῶτα.
pass_a_gloss: It is possible for us to divest ourselves of superfluity towards those who are fond of blame; for we are not children and infants in relation to the childish and easily despised learning, as those who have been brought to knowledge have slandered; for having been reborn, we have immediately received the perfect, on account of which we hasten. For we have been enlightened; and this is to know God. Therefore, the one who has known the perfect is not imperfect. And do not take hold of me as confessing that I have known God. For thus it seemed right to the Word to speak; and what is free. Immediately, therefore, when the Lord was being baptized from heaven, a voice sounded as a witness, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you.' Let us learn from the wise; today, having been reborn, is Christ already perfect or, which is absurd, imperfect? But if this, it is necessary for him to learn something. But it is not likely that he, being God, should learn even one thing. For no one would be greater than the Word, nor even a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not, therefore, confess against their will that the Word, perfect from the perfect Father, was reborn perfectly according to the economic pre-arrangement? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? It was necessary, they say, to fulfill the human promise. Beautifully, I say; for when he was being baptized by John, did he become perfect? It is clear that he did. Therefore, did he learn nothing in addition to this? No, he did not. For he is perfected by the bath alone and is sanctified by the descent of the Spirit; this is how it is. The same thing happens to us, of whom the Lord has become a guarantee; when we are baptized, we are enlightened, when we are enlightened, we are made sons, when we are made sons, we are perfected, when we are perfected, we are made immortal. 'I said', he says, 'you are gods and all sons of the Most High.' And this work is called by many names, a gift and enlightenment and perfection and bath; a bath, indeed, through which we wash away our sins, a gift by which the penalties for our sins are remitted, enlightenment through which that holy and saving light is beheld, that is, through which we perceive the divine; perfection, we say, is what is without need. For what is still lacking to the one who has known God? And it is also absurd that the gift of God should be called imperfect; but being perfect, he gives perfect gifts; just as all things come into being when he commands, so also it follows that when he gives, it is only necessary for him to will that the gift be fulfilled. For the future is anticipated by the power of his will. And the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only those, therefore, who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect; and we live, having already been separated from death. Salvation, therefore, is to follow Christ. 'For what has come into being in him is life.' 'Amen, amen, I say to you', he says, 'the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' Thus, to believe alone and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is never weak. Just as his will is a work and this is called the world, so also the will of God is the salvation of men, and this is called the church. He knows, therefore, those whom he has called, and those whom he has called, he has saved; and he has called and saved at the same time. 'For you are taught by God', the apostle says. It is not right, therefore, for us to think that what is taught by him is imperfect, but the lesson is eternal salvation from the eternal Savior, to whom be the glory forever, amen. And the one who has been reborn alone, as the name also has, having been enlightened, has immediately been freed from darkness and has received the light from that moment. Just as those who have shaken off sleep are immediately awake from within, or rather, just as those who try to remove the rheum from their eyes do not provide the light for themselves from outside, which they do not have, but by removing the obstacle from their sight, they leave their pupil free, so also those who are baptized, having wiped away the sins that overshadowed them like a cloud by the divine Spirit, we have a free and unobstructed and shining eye of the Spirit, by which alone we behold the divine, the Holy Spirit having come into us from heaven; this is the mixture of eternal light, able to see the eternal light; since what is like is friendly to what is like, and the holy is friendly to the one from whom the holy comes, which is properly called light; 'for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.' From this, I think that man has been called light by the ancients.
pass_b_english: We are free to set aside unnecessary defenses against those who love to find fault. We are neither children nor infants clinging to a childish, easily dismissed teaching, as those who claim superior knowledge have slandered us. On the contrary, having been reborn, we have immediately received the perfect goal toward which we press. We have been enlightened, and enlightenment is nothing other than knowing God. Therefore, the one who has known the perfect is not imperfect. Do not, however, seize on my words as a claim that I myself have fully known God. This is how the Word chose to speak—and the Word is free. Immediately upon the Lord's baptism, a voice from heaven bore witness: 'You are my beloved Son; today I have begotten you' (Matthew 3:17). Let us then learn from the wise: on the day he was reborn, was Christ already perfect, or—which is absurd—imperfect? If he were imperfect, he would need to learn something. But it is unthinkable that God would need to learn even a single thing. No one is greater than the Word, nor can anyone be a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not therefore be forced to confess that the Word, perfect from the perfect Father, was reborn perfectly according to the divine plan? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? 'To fulfill the human promise,' they say. Very well; then when he was baptized by John, did he become perfect? Clearly he did. So he learned nothing further? No, he did not. He is perfected by the bath alone and sanctified by the Spirit's descent. That is how it stands. The same sequence happens to us, for whom the Lord has become the guarantee: baptized, we are enlightened; enlightened, we are adopted as sons; adopted, we are perfected; perfected, we are made immortal. 'I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.' This work bears many names: gift, enlightenment, perfection, bath. It is a bath because through it we wash away our sins; a gift because through it the penalties due for our sins are remitted; enlightenment because through it that holy, saving light is beheld—that is, through it we perceive the divine. Perfection, we say, is what lacks nothing. What could still be lacking to the one who has known God? It is also absurd to call God's gift imperfect; being perfect, he gives perfect gifts. Just as all things come into being the moment he commands, so when he gives, it is only necessary for him to will that the gift be fulfilled. The future is anticipated by the power of his will. And the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only those who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect; and we live, having already been separated from death. Salvation, therefore, is to follow Christ. 'For what has come into being in him is life.' 'Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life' (John 5:24). Thus to believe and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is never weak. Just as his will is a work—and that work is called the world—so his will for humanity is salvation, and that salvation is called the church. He knows those he has called, and those he has called he has saved; he has called and saved at the same time. 'For you yourselves are taught by God,' the apostle says. It is not right, then, for us to suppose that what he teaches is imperfect. The lesson is eternal salvation from the eternal Savior, to whom be glory forever. Amen. And the one who has been reborn—true to the name—having been enlightened, is immediately freed from darkness and receives the light from that moment. Just as those who shake off sleep are instantly awake from within, or rather as those who try to remove the film from their eyes do not supply light from outside (for they do not possess it), but by removing the obstacle from their sight they leave the pupil free, so also the baptized, wiping away the sins that overshadowed them like a cloud by the divine Spirit, possess a free, unobstructed, radiant eye of the Spirit. By that eye alone we behold the divine, the Holy Spirit having entered us from heaven. This is the blend of eternal light, able to see the eternal light. For like is friendly to like, and the holy is friendly to the one from whom the holy comes—who is properly called Light. 'For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.' From this I conclude that man was called 'light' by the ancients.

review.notes: All clauses in the Greek were accounted for in Pass A and Pass B. Scripture citations were correctly identified and added in Pass B (Matthew 3:17, John 5:24) as required by the rules. The translation of 'ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα' as 'made immortal' is accurate. The title 'Perfection in Christ' captures the thought of the locus.
